Revelation — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

John's Revelation consists of two principal parts.

First, it concerns “the things that are”: the church's condition at the time.

It includes the apostle's vision of Jesus Christ, his command to write what he sees (Revelation 1:9–20), and the messages to the seven churches of Asia.

Those messages undoubtedly addressed the actual condition of each church then.

But their teachings, warnings, encouragements, praise, rebuke and promises are useful to the whole church in every age.

Second, Revelation describes “the things that will take place afterward”: prophecy concerning the church's future from the time John saw these visions.

This book is intended to promote spiritual growth.

It warns careless sinners, directs awakened people toward salvation, strengthens weak believers, comforts tempted and suffering Christians, and especially encourages martyrs faithful to Christ while enduring cruel persecution from Satan and his followers.

The revelation of Jesus Christ and its blessing (verses 1–3)

This book is the revelation of Jesus Christ. Indeed, all Scripture comes through him and ultimately concerns him.

Its chief purpose is to reveal God's intentions concerning the church and the nations in relation to it, continuing to the end of the world.

These events are certain to happen, and their fulfillment would begin soon.

Although Jesus is himself God, possessing light and life in himself, as Mediator he receives instructions from the Father to reveal to humanity.

Through Christ we know what to expect from God and what God requires from us.

The book pronounces a blessing on people who read and listen to its prophecy.

But merely hearing or reading is insufficient. Keep its message in memory, thought, affection and practice.

Even when the prophetic meaning is difficult, its mysteries reveal something of God, awaken reverence and purify the soul.

No other part of Scripture speaks more fully of the gospel or gives a stronger warning against sin.

Grace and peace from the Triune God (verses 4–8)

There is no true peace without grace. Where grace comes first, real peace follows.

John's greeting is an act of adoration to the Holy Trinity.

The Father is the eternal and unchanging Lord who is, was and is to come.

The Holy Spirit is described as the seven Spirits, the one perfect Spirit of God working through a diversity of gifts and operations.

Jesus Christ is the faithful Witness, the Firstborn from the dead and the Ruler over the earth's kings.

He knows all God's purposes and will raise his people by his own power.

Every ruler's plans are subject to him and every ruler must answer to him.

Sin stains the soul with guilt and corruption. Only Jesus' blood can remove that stain.

He shed his blood to satisfy divine justice, obtaining pardon and purification for his people.

He has made believers kings and priests.

As kings they overcome the world, put sin to death, govern their own hearts, resist Satan and prevail through prayer.

As priests they enter God's presence and offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable through Christ.

For these blessings, glory and rule belong to him forever.

Jesus will judge the world.

In the day of his appearing, everyone will see how wise and happy his friends were and how miserable his enemies are.

Henry warns that Christ's coming will terrify those who wound and crucify him by apostasy and astonish the ungodly world.

Remember his return often.

He is the Beginning and the End, the Almighty, the eternal and unchanging One from whom all things come and for whom they exist.

Anyone hoping to share his everlasting glory must willingly receive and honor him now as Savior, knowing he will return as Judge.

John sees the vision on the Lord's Day (verses 9–11)

John was suffering not for wrongdoing but for bearing witness to Jesus Christ, Emmanuel and Savior.

The Spirit of glory rested upon this persecuted apostle.

He received his vision on the Lord's Day, the first day of the week, which Henry identifies as the Christian Sabbath in remembrance of Christ's resurrection.

Those who call Jesus their Lord should honor him on his day.

Henry urges dedicating the Lord's Day wholly to spiritual duties, rather than spending its hours in sensual amusements or worldly pleasures.

John was in a serious, reverent and heavenly frame of mind through the Spirit's influence.

Believers seeking fellowship with God should turn thoughts and desires away from earthly distractions.

Sometimes Christians are prevented by necessity, not by choice, from joining public worship.

Even then they may find divine comfort through private prayer, meditation and the Spirit's presence.

Neither confinement nor external hardship can separate them from Christ's gracious voice and power.

John then heard a loud voice like a trumpet calling him.

The glorious Son of Man among his churches (verses 12–20)

The churches receive light from Jesus Christ and his gospel and are called to shine before others.

The golden lampstands picture their purity and value.

Not only ministers but all church members should live so that people glorify God.

Jesus stood among the lampstands, showing that he remains with his churches, filling them with light, life and love.

His long robe may signify righteousness and priestly mediation.

The golden sash may picture the preciousness of his love for his people.

His white hair may signify majesty, holiness and eternity.

His eyes like flame may show his knowledge of hearts and coming events.

His feet like refined bronze may show the firmness and excellence of his purposes and deeds.

His voice like rushing waters may reveal the irresistible power of his word.

The seven stars represent the ministers of the churches, whom Christ sustains and guides.

The sword represents his justice and the searching power of his word (Hebrews 4:12).

His face shone brighter than mortal eyes could bear.

Overwhelmed by this glory, John fell down.

We can be content to walk by faith during earthly life.

Jesus comforted John with “Do not fear.”

He revealed himself as the First and the Last, truly God.

He was once dead—the same One the disciples saw crucified—but now lives eternally, having overcome death.

He possesses supreme authority over death and the unseen world, judging with a sentence no one can overturn.

Listen to his voice, receive his love and obey his word.

What will he withhold from those for whom he gave his life?

Commit yourselves entirely to the One who rules all things wisely.

[Rev.1.1-Rev.1.3]
Revelation
The Book of the Revelation of St. John consists of two principal divisions. 1. Relates to "the things which are," that is, the then present state of the church, and contains the epistle of John to the seven churches, and his account of the appearance of the Lord Jesus, and his direction to the apostle to write what he beheld, ch. 1:9-20. Also the addresses or epistles to seven churches of Asia. These, doubtless, had reference to the state of the respective churches, as they then existed, but contain excellent precepts and exhortations, commendations and reproofs, promises and threatenings, suitable to instruct the Christian church at all times. 2. Contains a prophecy of "the things which shall be hereafter," and describes the future state of the church, from the time when the apostle beheld the visions here recorded. It is intended for our spiritual improvement; to warn the careless sinner, point out the way of salvation to the awakened inquirer, build up the weak believer, comfort the afflicted and tempted Christian, and, we may especially add, to strengthen the martyr of Christ, under the cruel persecutions and sufferings inflicted by Satan and his followers.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The Divine origin, the design, and the importance of this book. | (1-3) |
The apostle John salutes the seven churches of Asia. | (4-8) |
Declares when, where, and how, the revelation was made to him. | (9-11) |
His vision, in which he saw Christ appear. | (12-20) |
Verses 1-3
This book is the Revelation of Jesus Christ; the whole Bible is so; for all revelation comes through Christ, and all relates to him. Its principal subject is to discover the purposes of God concerning the affairs of the church, and of the nations as connected therewith, to the end of the world. These events would surely come to pass; and they would begin to come to pass very shortly. Though Christ is himself God, and has light and life in himself, yet, as Mediator between God and man, he receives instructions from the Father. To him we owe the knowledge of what we are to expect from God, and what he expects from us. The subject of this revelation was, the things that must shortly come to pass. On all who read or hear the words of the prophecy, a blessing is pronounced. Those are well employed who search the Bible. It is not enough that we read and hear, but we must keep the things that are written, in our memories, in our minds, in our affections, and in practice, and we shall be blessed in the deed. Even the mysteries and difficulties of this book are united with discoveries of God, suited to impress the mind with awe, and to purify the soul of the reader, though he may not discern the prophetic meaning. No part of Scripture more fully states the gospel, and warns against the evil of sin.
[Rev.1.4-Rev.1.8]
Verses 4-8
There can be no true peace, where there is not true grace; and where grace goeth before, peace will follow. This blessing is in the name of God, of the Holy Trinity, it is an act of adoration. The Father is first named; he is described as the Jehovah who is, and who was, and who is to come, eternal, unchangeable. The Holy Spirit is called the seven spirits, the perfect Spirit of God, in whom there is a diversity of gifts and operations. The Lord Jesus Christ was from eternity, a Witness to all the counsels of God. He is the First-born from the dead, who will by his own power raise up his people. He is the Prince of the kings of the earth; by him their counsels are overruled, and to him they are accountable. Sin leaves a stain of guilt and pollution upon the soul. Nothing can fetch out this stain but the blood of Christ; and Christ shed his own blood to satisfy Divine justice, and purchase pardon and purity for his people. Christ has made believers kings and priests to God and his Father. As such they overcome the world, mortify sin, govern their own spirits, resist Satan, prevail with God in prayer, and shall judge the world. He has made them priests, given them access to God, enabled them to offer spiritual and acceptable sacrifices, and for these favours they are bound to ascribe to him dominion and glory for ever. He will judge the world. Attention is called to that great day when all will see the wisdom and happiness of the friends of Christ, and the madness and misery of his enemies. Let us think frequently upon the second coming of Christ. He shall come, to the terror of those who wound and crucify him by apostacy: he shall come, to the astonishment of the whole world of the ungodly. He is the Beginning and the End; all things are from him and for him; he is the Almighty; the same eternal and unchanged One. And if we would be numbered with his saints in glory everlasting, we must now willing submit to him receive him, and honour him as a saviour, who we believe will come to be our Judge. Alas, that there should be many, who would wish never to die, and that there should not be a day of judgment!
[Rev.1.9-Rev.1.11]
Verses 9-11
It was the apostle's comfort that he did not suffer as an evil-doer, but for the testimony of Jesus, for bearing witness to Christ as the Immanuel, the Saviour; and the Spirit of glory and of God rested upon this persecuted apostle. The day and time when he had this vision was the Lord's day, the Christian sabbath, the first day of the week, observed in remembrance of the resurrection of Christ. Let us who call him "Our Lord," honour him on his own day. The name shows how this sacred day should be observed; the Lord's day should be wholly devoted to the Lord, and none of its hours employed in a sensual, worldly manner, or in amusements. He was in a serious, heavenly, spiritual frame, under the gracious influences of the Spirit of God. Those who would enjoy communion with God on the Lord's day, must seek to draw their thoughts and affections from earthly things. And if believers are kept on the Lord's holy day, from public ordinances and the communion of saints, by necessity and not by choice, they may look for comfort in meditation and secret duties, from the influences of the Spirit; and by hearing the voice and contemplating the glory of their beloved Saviour, from whose gracious words and power no confinement or outward circumstances can separate them. An alarm was given as with the sound of the trumpet, and then the apostle heard the voice of Christ.
[Rev.1.12-Rev.1.20]
Verses 12-20
The churches receive their light from Christ and the gospel, and hold it forth to others. They are golden candlesticks; they should be precious and pure; not only the ministers, but the members of the churches; their light should so shine before men, as to engage others to give glory to God. And the apostle saw as though of the Lord Jesus Christ appeared in the midst of the golden candlesticks. He is with his churches always, to the end of the world, filling them with light, and life, and love. He was clothed with a robe down to the feet, perhaps representing his righteousness and priesthood, as Mediator. This vest was girt with a golden girdle, which may denote how precious are his love and affection for his people. His head and hairs white like wool and as snow, may signify his majesty, purity, and eternity. His eyes as a flame of fire, may represent his knowledge of the secrets of all hearts, and of the most distant events. His feet like fine brass burning in a furnace, may denote the firmness of his appointments, and the excellence of his proceedings. His voice as the sound of many waters, may represent the power of his word, to remove or to destroy. The seven stars were emblems of the ministers of the seven churches to which the apostle was ordered to write, and whom Christ upheld and directed. The sword represented his justice, and his word, piercing to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, [Heb.4.12] He 4:12. His countenance was like the sun, when it shines clearly and powerfully; its strength too bright and dazzling for mortal eyes to behold. The apostle was overpowered with the greatness of the lustre and glory in which Christ appeared. We may well be contented to walk by faith, while here upon earth. The Lord Jesus spake words of comfort; Fear not. Words of instruction; telling who thus appeared. And his Divine nature; the First and the Last. His former sufferings; I was dead: the very same whom his disciples saw upon the cross. His resurrection and life; I have conquered death, and am partaker of endless life. His office and authority; sovereign dominion in and over the invisible world, as the Judge of all, from whose sentence there is no appeal. Let us listen to the voice of Christ, and receive the tokens of his love, for what can he withhold from those for whose sins he has died? May we then obey his word, and give up ourselves wholly to him who directs all things aright.

Ephesus: return to your first love (verses 1–7)

The churches differed greatly in purity of teaching and genuine godliness.

Christ's messages to them therefore continue speaking to churches and believers in every age.

Although Jesus reigns in heaven, he walks among the churches on earth, observing their strengths, weaknesses and needs.

He commended Ephesus for diligent service.

Christ remembers every hour of work his servants perform; no faithful labor is wasted.

But diligence alone is not sufficient. We also need patience in suffering and patience in waiting.

Although Christians owe gentleness to people, they must not be indifferent to sin.

The Ephesian church had not ceased loving Christ altogether. It had lost the intensity of its first love.

Christ is displeased when believers become cold and careless toward him.

Calling this decline harmless or normal excuses a sin Christ requires us to repent of.

The church should grieve over this spiritual cooling, confess it humbly and recover its former zeal, prayerfulness and watchfulness.

Indifference toward truth and error, good and evil, may be mislabeled charity, but it is not Christian charity.

The Christian life remains a struggle against sin, Satan, the world and the flesh.

Persevering believers receive the promised Tree of Life, not merely a return to Eden but perfect, everlasting joy in heaven.

During earthly life, anticipate that joy through faith, fellowship with Christ and the Spirit's comforts.

Do not expect uninterrupted peace or freedom from spiritual conflict before heaven.

Smyrna: remain faithful through suffering (verses 8–11)

Jesus is the First, because he created everything and existed before all things, with God and himself God.

He is the Last, because he will judge everyone.

The One who died and lives again is the suffering believer's Brother and Friend.

Consequently even people in severe poverty may be spiritually rich, honored amid humiliation and happy under trials.

Some wealthy people are spiritually destitute. Some outwardly poor Christians are rich in faith, good works, privileges, gifts and hope.

When people lose earthly possessions for Christ and a clear conscience, he makes up for the loss through spiritual wealth.

Jesus arms his people against approaching trials: Do not fear.

He not only commands courage but supplies strength to practice it.

The trials were permitted to test, not destroy, his faithful people.

His promised crown of life is certain and fitting: a life exhausted or surrendered for Christ is rewarded with a far greater, eternal life.

The second death is immeasurably more terrible than bodily death because it is everlasting. Henry describes its terror as dying and always dying.

Those spared that judgment through Christ can patiently bear any suffering encountered in this world.

Pergamum: reject false liberty and hold fast (verses 12–17)

God's word is a two-edged sword, able to strike at both sin and sinners.

Believers need not fear the sword of Christ's judgment if they remain obedient.

Jesus knows both the opportunities and the temptations arising from the places where his people live.

Pergamum remained faithful through difficult trials, refusing both open apostasy and accommodation merely to avoid suffering.

Christ commended its faithfulness but rebuked its failure to confront false teaching.

A distorted understanding of Christian liberty can become a bitter root from which serious sin grows.

Repentance is required not only of individuals but also of congregations and communities that sin together.

The conqueror receives Christ's hidden spiritual nourishment and consolations, unknown to the world.

The new name signifies adoption into God's family.

The Holy Spirit makes believers understand the reality of this new identity through the work he has performed in their hearts.

Thyatira: love must not tolerate corrupt teaching (verses 18–29)

Jesus notices good works born of love, faith, zeal and patience.

Yet his flaming eyes also see any wrongdoing the church permits.

He rebukes, disciplines or judges such evil.

He praised Thyatira's ministers and members for growth in goodness and wisdom.

All Christians should desire their latest works to be their best works.

But the church tolerated people who seduced others into wickedness.

By judging deceivers, Christ shows that he knows hearts, motives, plans and the hidden spirit of every person.

Those remaining undefiled receive encouragement.

It is dangerous to disregard God's mysteries; it is also dangerous to become fascinated by Satan's supposed secret depths.

The less experience believers have of his deceits, the better.

Christ cares tenderly for his faithful servants and imposes no burden that is not for their good.

He promises rich reward to those who persevere, including fitting wisdom and authority.

Christ brings the dawn of grace and glory into the soul and gives himself for its enjoyment.

After every spiritual victory, continue resisting the enemy until the end.

Verses 1-7
These churches were in such different states as to purity of doctrine and the power of godliness, that the words of Christ to them will always suit the cases of other churches, and professors. Christ knows and observes their state; though in heaven, yet he walks in the midst of his churches on earth, observing what is wrong in them, and what they want. The church of Ephesus is commended for diligence in duty. Christ keeps an account of every hour's work his servants do for him, and their labour shall not be in vain in the Lord. But it is not enough that we are diligent; there must be bearing patience, and there must be waiting patience. And though we must show all meekness to all men, yet we must show just zeal against their sins. The sin Christ charged this church with, is, not the having left and forsaken the object of love, but having lost the fervent degree of it that at first appeared. Christ is displeased with his people, when he sees them grow remiss and cold toward him. Surely this mention in Scripture, of Christians forsaking their first love, reproves those who speak of it with carelessness, and thus try to excuse indifference and sloth in themselves and others; our Saviour considers this indifference as sinful. They must repent: they must be grieved and ashamed for their sinful declining, and humbly confess it in the sight of God. They must endeavour to recover their first zeal, tenderness, and seriousness, and must pray as earnestly, and watch as diligently, as when they first set out in the ways of God. If the presence of Christ's grace and Spirit is slighted, we may expect the presence of his displeasure. Encouraging mention is made of what was good among them. Indifference as to truth and error, good and evil, may be called charity and meekness, but it is not so; and it is displeasing to Christ. The Christian life is a warfare against sin, Satan, the world, and the flesh. We must never yield to our spiritual enemies, and then we shall have a glorious triumph and reward. All who persevere, shall derive from Christ, as the Tree of life, perfection and confirmation in holiness and happiness, not in the earthly paradise, but in the heavenly. This is a figurative expression, taken from the account of the garden of Eden, denoting the pure, satisfactory, and eternal joys of heaven; and the looking forward to them in this world, by faith, communion with Christ, and the consolations of the Holy Spirit. Believers, take your wrestling life here, and expect and look for a quiet life hereafter; but not till then: the word of God never promises quietness and complete freedom from conflict here.
[Rev.2.8-Rev.2.11]
Verses 8-11
Our Lord Jesus is the First, for by him were all things made; he was before all things, with God, and is God himself. He is the Last, for he will be the Judge of all. As this First and Last, who was dead and is alive, is the believer's Brother and Friend, he must be rich in the deepest poverty, honourable amidst the lowest abasement, and happy under the heaviest tribulation, like the church of Smyrna. Many who are rich as to this world, are poor as to the next; and some who are poor outwardly, are inwardly rich; rich in faith, in good works, rich in privileges, rich in gifts, rich in hope. Where there is spiritual plenty, outward poverty may be well borne; and when God's people are made poor as to this life, for the sake of Christ and a good conscience, he makes all up to them in spiritual riches. Christ arms against coming troubles. Fear none of these things; not only forbid slavish fear, but subdue it, furnishing the soul with strength and courage. It should be to try them, not to destroy them. Observe, the sureness of the reward; "I will give thee:" they shall have the reward from Christ's own hand. Also, how suitable it is; "a crown of life:" the life worn out in his service, or laid down in his cause, shall be rewarded with a much better life, which shall be eternal. The second death is unspeakably worse than the first death, both in the agonies of it, and as it is eternal death: it is indeed awful to die, and to be always dying. If a man is kept from the second death and wrath to come, he may patiently endure whatever he meets with in this world.
[Rev.2.12-Rev.2.17]
Verses 12-17
The word of God is a sword, able to slay both sin and sinners. It turns and cuts every way; but the believer need not fear this sword; yet this confidence cannot be supported without steady obedience. As our Lord notices all the advantages and opportunities we have for duty in the places where we dwell, so he notices our temptations and discouragements from the same causes. In a situation of trials, the church of Pergamos had not denied the faith, either by open apostacy, or by giving way so as to avoid the cross. Christ commends their stedfastness, but reproves their sinful failures. A wrong view of gospel doctrine and Christian liberty, was a root of bitterness from which evil practices grew. Repentance is the duty of churches and bodies of men, as well as of particular persons; those who sin together, should repent together. Here is the promise of favour to those that overcome. The influences and comforts of the Spirit of Christ, come down from heaven into the soul, for its support. This is hidden from the rest of the world. The new name is the name of adoption; when the Holy Spirit shows his own work in the believer's soul, this new name and its real import are understood by him.
[Rev.2.18-Rev.2.29]
Verses 18-29
Even when the Lord knows the works of his people to be wrought in love, faith, zeal, and patience; yet if his eyes, which are as a flame of fire, observe them committing or allowing what is evil, he will rebuke, correct, or punish them. Here is praise of the ministry and people of Thyatira, by One who knew the principles from which they acted. They grew wiser and better. All Christians should earnestly desire that their last works may be their best works. Yet this church connived at some wicked seducers. God is known by the judgments he executes; and by this upon seducers, he shows his certain knowledge of the hearts of men, of their principles, designs, frame, and temper. Encouragement is given to those who kept themselves pure and undefiled. It is dangerous to despise the mystery of God, and as dangerous to receive the mysteries of Satan. Let us beware of the depths of Satan, of which those who know the least are the most happy. How tender Christ is of his faithful servants! He lays nothing upon his servants but what is for their good. There is promise of an ample reward to the persevering, victorious believer; also knowledge and wisdom, suitable to their power and dominion. Christ brings day with him into the soul, the light of grace and of glory, in the presence and enjoyment of him their Lord and Saviour. After every victory let us follow up our advantage against the enemy, that we may overcome and keep the works of Christ to the end.

Sardis: wake up and strengthen what remains (verses 1–6)

Jesus Christ possesses the Holy Spirit, with all the Spirit's powers, graces and operations.

He knows his churches and all their works. He exposed the hypocrisy and terrible spiritual decline of Sardis.

Outwardly, the church seemed healthy. Inwardly, much of its religion was only a form of godliness without its power: it had a reputation for life but lacked the principle of life itself.

Many members were hypocrites altogether; others retained spiritual life but had fallen into weakness and disorder.

Christ therefore called them to wakefulness, watchfulness and energetic obedience. They were to depend on the Holy Spirit's grace to revive faith and holy affections and to strengthen those who had not yet died spiritually.

Whenever we stop watching, we lose ground.

Their works were unfinished and hollow. Prayers lacked sincere holy desires, acts of giving lacked genuine love, and Sabbath observance lacked fitting devotion of heart.

Their outward forms did not match their inward condition; once the spirit of worship is missing, its forms cannot continue for long.

To seek revival in ourselves and others, we must compare what we profess with how we actually live. This should humble us, awaken us and move us to hold firmly to what remains.

Christ warns of severe consequences for ignoring his counsel, yet he does not leave the church without hope.

He remembers the faithful remnant at Sardis and promises them honor.

Those who overcome will receive white clothing: the purity of grace perfected in the purity of glory.

Christ holds the book of life, remembering all who will inherit eternal life and those who maintain genuine devotion amid evil times.

On the great day, he will acknowledge the names of his faithful people before God and all the angels.

Philadelphia: the open door and enduring faithfulness (verses 7–13)

Jesus Christ holds the key of authority and government over the church.

He opens opportunities for his congregations, opens doors for his ministers to speak, and opens hearts to receive his word.

He also shuts heaven's door to those who waste their time of grace in spiritual sleep and to those who continue in evil, however confident they may seem.

Philadelphia received praise, though also a gentle correction.

Christ accepts a little strength, but believers must never be content to remain weak. They should grow in grace, become strong in faith and bring glory to God.

Christ can display his favor so clearly that even enemies of his people must acknowledge it.

Through grace their opposition may soften, and they may desire fellowship with those they once opposed.

He promises to preserve faithful believers in their hardest trials.

Those who have kept his gospel in times of peace will find that he sustains them during temptation and persecution.

The same grace that made them fruitful in peaceful days will enable them to remain faithful in suffering.

Christ promises an enduring reward to those who overcome.

He will make them pillars in God's temple, monuments to his free and powerful grace that will never be destroyed or removed.

His new name written upon them will identify the Lord under whose leadership they fought and won their spiritual battle.

Laodicea: repent of complacency and welcome Christ (verses 14–22)

Laodicea was the last and worst of the seven churches of Asia.

Jesus calls himself the Amen: unwavering in his purposes and faithful to all his promises.

If religion matters at all, it matters supremely. Christ requires earnest devotion.

Yet many who profess the gospel are neither hot nor cold. They show little concern for essential matters while becoming angry and combative about minor disputes.

Christ warns such people of severe judgment.

Their indifference gives others a false picture of Christianity. Some conclude that the faith is unholy; others suppose it cannot bring real satisfaction, since its professed followers are so lifeless and quick to seek happiness from the world.

Self-conceit and self-deception are among the roots of this spiritual inconsistency.

What a difference between Laodicea's opinion of itself and Christ's judgment of it!

We must not deceive our own souls. Henry warns that many are in hell who once believed themselves far along the road to heaven.

Pray earnestly that God will keep us from flattering ourselves.

People grow proud as religion becomes outward and worldly.

The Laodiceans imagined themselves rich, yet were spiritually poor; they believed they could see, but were blind to their condition and danger.

They lacked the clothing of justification and sanctification. Exposed to sin and shame, they were naked, without the shelter of God in whom alone the soul finds lasting safety.

Christ nevertheless offered them the counsel they needed.

He revealed where genuine riches could be found and how to receive them.

They must relinquish sin and self-confidence, not anything truly valuable, so that they might receive the treasures he gives.

From Christ they must receive white clothing: his righteousness counted as theirs for justification, together with holiness and sanctification.

By yielding to his word and Spirit, they would receive sight to recognize their way and their final destination.

Let us examine ourselves by the standard of Scripture and ask the Holy Spirit to remove pride, prejudice and worldly desire.

Sinners should receive the rebukes of God's word and correcting providence as signs of concern for their souls.

Christ stands at the door and knocks through providential events, Scripture's warnings and teaching, and the influences of his Spirit.

Those who open to him enjoy his fellowship.

What we offer him may be a poor meal, but what he brings supplies a rich feast of fresh grace and consolation.

Christ overcame every temptation and conflict he faced.

Those who are made like him in his trials will also be made like him in glory, sharing his promised victory.

The final call to listen belongs not only to these seven congregations, but to everyone.

And, observe, of those who are thus sealed by the Spirit, the seal must be on the forehead, plainly to be seen alike by friends and foes, but not by the believer himself, except as he looks stedfastly in the glass of God's word. The number of those who were sealed, may be understood to stand for the remnant of people which God reserved. Verses 7-13
The first angel sounded the first trumpet, and there followed hail and fire mingled with blood. A storm of heresies, a mixture of dreadful errors falling on the church, or a tempest of destruction. The second angel sounded, and a great mountain, burning with fire, was cast into the sea; and the third part of the sea became blood. By this mountain some understand leaders of the persecutions; others, Rome sacked by the Goths and Vandals, with great slaughter and cruelty. God gives alarm by the written word, by ministers, by men's own consciences, and by the signs of the times; so that if people are surprised, it is their own fault. The anger of God makes all comforts bitter, and even life itself burdensome. But God, in this world, sets bounds to the most terrible judgments.
